The future Liverpool legend was born and raised in Glasgow

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

During his 22-year playing career, Kenny Dalglish became one of the greatest players in British football history.

After winning no less than four Scottish titles and another four Scottish Cups with Celtic, Dalglish made the move south of the border in 1977, where his achievements with Liverpool outstripped even those he accomplished at Celtic Park.

But it was in Glasgow where the foundations of this great career were laid, from Sunday morning kickabouts and makeshift goalposts and onto amatuer football and apprenticeships.

“My dad took me to the football when I was a wee boy, so I started to get into it and we had a bit of grass in the back garden, six-by-six – after the game, I'd go back and have a kickabout there with my dad,” Dalglish reminises to FourFourTwo. “He was a Rangers fan, so he took me there – my first hero was a player that no-one would have heard of now, a centre-forward named Don Kitchenbrand. I thought, ‘He must be good, he scores goals all the time!'

While Dalglish would end his career with almost 350 goals, he started further back on the pitch.

“When I was seven, I played as a goalkeeper before moving outfield – one of the boys' dads must have been a plumber, because they used to get these wee poles and fit posts onto a crossbar, then got nets from somewhere,” he continues.

“That was our wee team on a Sunday. “Why did I become a good player? I never thought I was that good – it was for other people to think that. A lot of people help you on the way – the most important person is the one who starts you off, and that was my dad. I'd play for school on a Saturday morning, then my amateur club in the afternoon. Mum was there too – there was never enough money, so if there was a tear in a sock, the mothers were there with a knitting needle. They took turns washing the strips as well. It was really communal.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“When I was 14, we moved to high-rise flats near Ibrox. I was about to leave school – you left at 15 then – and I'd been playing football with the school, as well as an amateur club, Possil YM. I got into the Glasgow Schools under-13s, under-14s and under-15s teams – I could have gone to a new school near the flats we moved to, but thought, ‘I've been to my school since I was young, I don't want another one to get the credit.'

“It was only right that the school where I was educated – supposedly! – was where I got into the Scottish squad. “The guy who took the Glasgow team was very prominent with the Scottish schoolboys – they got beat once, so he said, ‘This boy could come and play.'

“Then when you're leaving school, they put a piece of paper in front of you and say, ‘Get yourself a job.' That was a very limited choice for me, but my first job was as a van boy, delivering school books – they were educational books, but I never read any of them!

“At my amateur club Glasgow United, we had a really good team and you could join a professional club at 15 as an apprentice, but I thought it would be more advantageous to try to get a trade instead. At a club, all you were doing in the summer was painting the crossbar or the terraces, doing something to help the groundsman.

“I thought it would be a good idea to have a trade, so I got a job as an apprentice joiner. At that point, I was training twice a week with a semi-professional team, Cumbernauld United, but if I wasn't going to be a footballer, at least I'd have had something to fall back on.

“I’d be a tradesman. It's just as well as football worked out for me, because I wasn't much cop with a saw and chisel…”

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#980. McAteer 'intelligence' earns praise from Ipswich boss

Mary McAteer celebrates after scoring Ipswich's opening goal at Watford

Ipswich Town boss David Wright praised the football intelligence of Wales international Mary McAteer following her first goal for the club.

McAteer joined Town on loan from Charlton Athletic in September as part of a revamp of the squad following last season's ninth-place finish in Women's Super League 2.

She headed home the rebound after skipper Maria Boswell's fierce shot came back off the crossbar against Watford and they went on to win Sunday's game 2-1.

The victory put Town third - and in the play-off places - in only their second season at that level.

"Every time Bos gets the ball in that area now, in my head I'm thinking, 'just shoot'," Wright told BBC Radio Suffolk.

"Mary is a really intelligent footballer - she uses her intelligence to find space between the lines, it allows her link through the thirds, and it's another sign of her intelligence that when Bos hits a beautiful strike, it hits the bar, bounces down, she's the first one to react and nods it in."

Ipswich on 'inevitable' path to WSL - Boswell

Kit Graham added Ipswich's second as they bounced back positively from a 2-1 home league defeat by Bristol City and midweek loss to McAteer's parent club Charlton in the Players' Cup.

"It has been a really tough week, not just physically, but also psychologically - three different challenges," said Wright.

"What good teams do is they bounce back. To finish the week off, going to Watford and coming away with three points, the girls should be really proud of themselves."

Boswell said last month that she believes it is "inevitable" that Town will eventually achieve their goal of a place in the top flight of English women's football.

But despite their current position, Wright insisted it was not a focus for him.

"I don't really look at the table. I want to push them, make them better and if we do that we will keep moving in the right direction - that process is getting better every day and will help us achieve what we want to achieve," he said.

Wright's side have won five of their eight WSL 2 games but now have over a month to wait before the next, when they travel to bottom-of-the-table Durham.

"I was looking at the calendar on the wall and I've never known such a big gap. The good thing is we've got lots of games in between so we'll be busy and when the Durham game comes round, the girls will be ready," Wright added.

#979. Portugal did the extraordinary with Cristiano Ronaldo. Can they do it without him?

The captain, the talisman, the brand: former teammates and experts discuss Portugal entering a new era after 23 years

There are days football fans hope will never come. For Portugal, this is one of them. For 23 years, Cristiano Ronaldo has been more than the country’s greatest footballer; he has been its defining sporting figure, a symbol of national pride and constant presence in the lives of supporters. After 234 appearances and 146 goals, the No 7 brought that chapter to a close and on Saturday night the team will play their first game without him.

The national side are losing more than a great footballer; they are also losing one of the world’s biggest brands. Daniel Sá, the executive director of the Portuguese institute of marketing administration, believes Portugal require reinvention to attract at least some of the millions of viewers who tuned in because of CR7.

“According to our latest evaluation, his brand alone is worth €850m (£710m),” he says. “People identify with his story: a young boy who travelled to Lisbon alone, lost his father and achieved success through his own hard work. Portugal has a long history of great players but no one has ever enjoyed this kind of global exposure. From a marketing standpoint, I have absolutely no doubt that most of the world watched Portugal’s matches because of Cristiano Ronaldo.”

Leonel Pontes, the technical director at Shanghai Shenhua, sees this reality in his everyday life. Pontes played an important role in shaping Ronaldo’s career at Sporting’s academy and became a mentor, helping the teenager from Madeira to cope with homesickness. He later coached Ronaldo as Portugal’s assistant manager and has been in China since 2023.

“When I tell people here in China that I’m Portuguese, the first thing they talk about is Cristiano,” Pontes says. “Just earlier this week, I visited an exhibition about his career here in Shanghai. I think his departure from the national team, which was always going to happen sooner or later, wasn’t handled properly. There were mistakes on both sides [by the player and the coach] but the country missed an opportunity to pay tribute to everything he has given us.”

So, what do the national team, who host Denmark in Braga, have left? A wealth of talent, certainly. Vitinha, Bruno Fernandes, João Neves, Nuno Mendes and Diogo Costa are some of the most prominent names in a squad packed with technical quality and tactical intelligence.

Petit, who played with Ronaldo for Portugal between 2003 and 2008 and manages the Azores club Santa Clara, says that talent must take responsibility. “Ronaldo could single-handedly solve a difficult game inside the box, with a free-kick or with another set piece. We, as teammates, were aware of it. But now we have great players from top clubs, they need to stand up. For some of them, this could be their last chance [for international success]. We are getting some younger players now. But Portugal has style and game ideas to be able to reach success.”

Replacing Ronaldo will mean more than finding someone capable of scoring his goals or wearing the No 7 shirt. He has been part of what it has meant to support Portugal. Fans grew up watching him, celebrating with him and, through the disappointments and triumphs, believing their national team could achieve something extraordinary with him leading the way. The country will move on but the era he leaves behind will be extraordinarily difficult to replicate.

Pontes, who assisted Paulo Bento with Portugal between 2010 and 2014, says: “He sacrificed a great deal for the national team. He played injured, he played when he wasn’t fully fit, but he was always there. He always gave his best.”

Ronaldo’s commitment to the game and love for Portugal was clear to Dany Mota, a Monza forward who trained with him at Juventus and with the national team. “When I arrived at Juventus, I had already heard the saying: ‘First to arrive at the training ground, last to leave.’ I wanted to see it for myself. So, one morning, I arrived really early, went to the gym, and there he was, already working out. After a few particularly demanding days, you would naturally start to feel a little tired or less motivated but that never seemed to happen to him. He would still be swimming, running or lifting weights in the gym. He was a machine and had an endless love for the national team.”

Portugal were blessed with talent before Ronaldo but major honours remained elusive. The so-called Golden Generation, featuring Luís Figo, Rui Costa and João Pinto, reached the semi-finals of Euro 2000 and, with a young Ronaldo, the final of Euro 2004, only to fall short. For Portugal supporters, there was a growing feeling that if the country was to triumph, it had to be with Ronaldo leading the way. He used defeat by Greece in the Euro 2004 final, on home soil, as fuel.

“He had a very particular ability to turn frustration into a desire to improve,” says Maniche, who shared the dressing room with Ronaldo during Portugal’s greatest football disappointment. “That characteristic has stayed with him throughout his career. Talent can open many doors, but it is that mentality that allows you to remain at the top for so many years.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

After Ronaldo’s 2004 tears of disappointment came tears of joy 12 years later when Portugal won the Euros in arguably the defining moment of his international career. Ronaldo was forced off injured against France but from the sidelines he encouraged his teammates, celebrated every intervention and experienced the final with the intensity of someone who understood what victory would mean to his country.

Millions around the world have identified deeply with Ronaldo’s journey. He embodies the fact that, regardless of where you come from or how difficult your circumstances, dedication, self-belief and an unwavering determination can take you further than anyone might have imagined. From a modest upbringing, with a father battling alcoholism, he has reached the pinnacle of football.

“When I first took him to the airport so he could fly back to Madeira for Christmas, I was afraid he wouldn’t come back,” Pontes recalls. “But he did. I’ve coached a lot of kids but Cristiano had two qualities I’d never seen in anyone else. First, he had a natural leadership ability and an extraordinary influence over his teammates, driven by his technical quality and fearlessness. Second, he possessed an exceptional mechanical understanding of his own body. He knew exactly how to position himself to achieve what he wanted, whether that meant adjusting his movement or striking the ball.”

At 41, his club career – with Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia – has no end in sight. What still drives him, apart from the objective of scoring 1,000 career goals?

“It is a competitive mentality deeply ingrained in his personality,” Maniche says. “It is about the challenge of continuing to prove to yourself that you are good enough, that you can push beyond your own limits and sustain an extraordinary level of performance.”

Portugal did the extraordinary with Ronaldo. Can they do it without him?

The former Sunderland stopper trained alongside the ex-Manchester United great with Denmark

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For many, Peter Schmeichel was the greatest goalkeeper of his generation.

The Dane enjoyed a trophy-laden career with Manchester United and also played a huge part in helping his country to a remarkable European Championship victory in 1992.

Schmeichel would eventually be succeeded as Denmark’s No. 1 by Thomas Sorensen, with the former Sunderland stopper able able to benefit from training alongside his legendary compatriot.

“There was nothing better than watching him train,” Sorensen tells FourFourTwo. “It was great because you could see him firsthand and get a lot of experience.

There were times, however, when Schmeichel’s formidable reputation came to the fore at training.

“It was also pretty intimidating,” Sorensen adds. “He could be quite rough sometimes. He’d put me in my place. One day he’d be my best friend and the next he wouldn’t even say, ‘Good morning’ to me.”

But as the pair have got old, this relationship has mellowed.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“He was a strange character in some ways, but I’ve gotten to know him a lot better over the years and I’m still good friends with his son Kasper,” he adds. “He’s totally different now than he was in his playing days.”

Schmeichel called time on his international career in 2001, leaving Sorensen with the somewhat tough task of replacing an all-time great in the Danish team.

“It wasn’t just me – there were a few of us dubbed ‘The next Peter Schmeichel’,” Sorensen recalls.

“I ended up being the winning horse. From the outset, I knew I was different from him and wanted to do it my way. He was very loud, outspoken and aggressive on the pitch. I was a little bit calmer.

“I came in at the right time because I’ve spoken to a lot of goalkeepers who were in his shadow for years and never got the chance. It probably wasn’t as hard as people think. We had success as a team and I played some good games. That always helps.

“He wasn’t forgotten, but that changeover was accepted pretty quickly.”

#976. 'I persuaded my club to give me a job as a content creator'

If someone would've said to me I'd be doing this as a job when I was 12, I wouldn't have believed them.

My name's Jacob. I'm a content creator, and I work with Bolton Wanderers.

My role here at Bolton is coming up with new ideas for social media, to try new concepts, filming stuff, and then posting them onto Bolton's pages and trying to help people follow the club. In my opinion, I think it's one of the funnest jobs in football, and it's brilliant.

Right. Welcome to Bolton, Larra. I hope I said that right. I'm going to teach you some Bolton twang to help you settle in.

My passion for football when I was growing up started at a very young age. My dad used to take me to the football matches, and I got my very first season ticket when I was five years old in the 2010/11 season, when Bolton was in the Premiership. Being something I loved as a kid, to turn it into my job is amazing.

I work here at least two days a week, obviously filming content, producing content,and then on match day, I'll be filming mostly with fans, and I love it.

As a town? Well, for us, it's lovely. Yeah.

Mondays, meetings. We have the marketing meeting, so that gives you an idea of what the week holds, what I'm going to do on a match day with the fans. And then in the week, I either film in with players, retail, commercial,whatever department needs help producing videos.

Some of the skills I use, I think one of them's got to be communication. You've got to be able to talk to people, talk to fans, and if you're watching this and you're a bit shy, or you think you can't communicate with people as well, I was like that inhigh school, so you learn it as you get older. But working in football, you've got to be adaptable because one minute you're doing a new signing, next minute you're working with the players, next minute it's a match day, next minute the season's over.

I'd say another one is being creative. That's probably the most important one because without being creative, you won't be able to put a video together.

So when I was 16 in high school, that's where my journey started. I did videos, which got me a number of followers. I always struggled in the classroom side in high school, but creating content and creating ideas and being creative, I was always really, really good at in high school, whether that would be doing something drama-related or English, writing, creating stories. I always knew I had a passion for creative pieces of work and being able to now do it as a job, it suits me down to the ground.

I didn't go to college. I didn't go to uni. I left high school with no GCSEs, but I've always had a real passion for football, so that's how I got in contact with Bolton Wanderers. I started doing some videos here at Bolton with the fans and that, and then it turned into going to the training ground and filming with the players, working with the commercial team, retail team, all the different departmentsaround the football club to eventually getting a paid role in football.

I think don't wait for an opportunity to come to you. Get out there and try. If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role there. But if it doesn't, then you've also created a portfolio working with different people, different businesses, different companies, and it's really good for your CV and for future opportunities with different companies.

The highlight of my career so far, probably looking back, being resilient enough to create my own career path in doing something I love.

When you score this season, you might be chuffed.

If you're passionate about football, you're a bit creative, and you're good in front of the camera, content creation infootball might be a job for you.

To find out what other careers you can have in football, explore the BBC Bitesize Follow Your Passion collection.

Making videos with fans and players at his local football club is all in a day's work for Jacob.

He's a content creator for Bolton Wanderers FC, coming up with new ideas for social media, filming videos and posting them onto official pages. The aim is to encourage people to follow the club.

There are many different ways to develop a career in football content creation, from apprenticeships to freelance work and full-time employment. It isn't just about making videos - content creators need to understanding their audience, respond to analytics and adapt material for different platforms

Jacob works as a content creator for Bolton Wanderers and his career progression has followed this path:

Voluntary work at Bolton --> Professional content creator

While it might look simple, he's had to be resilient - and one of the biggest obstacles he faced was convincing Bolton to create his role. "Don't wait for an opportunity to come to you," he says. "If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role. If it doesn't, you've created a portfolio and it's really good for your CV and future opportunities."

Jacob says salaries can range from Â£26,000 to around Â£40,000 for roles like his. Like him, some content creators start by doing it as a hobby while they improve their skills. While some content creators are full-time employees, many are freelancers so their average salaries can be variable.

Find out more about the role of a content creator below. Content creation roles can come under a range of titles including social media manager or content manager.

You could get into this role via a college course (to get practical skills in video editing and production, or a T Level in Marketing), an apprenticeship, volunteering, short private training courses and also teaching yourself.

#974. How to become a football referee

Honestly, for me it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done. You find so much more out about yourself that you probably never knew.

Louise Thompson, women's referee pathway officer for the Irish Football Association, international FIFA referee, and PremierLeague referee in Northern Ireland.

What does a women's referee pathway officer do?

Looking after female referees within Northern Ireland, trying to recruit, retain and give them experience within their games to pushthrough into top level refereeing.

What kind of training do you give to aspiring referees?

So from going through recruitment courses first of all, and then we do the beginners course with referees, just giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge, then we will also do a practical part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we'll go through scenarios, positioning, things around free kick management for example, other set pieces likecorners, penalty setup, what you do as a referee day to day, even pre match stuff as well, so when you arrive at the grounds, how you check the pitch, check all the equipment is there, how you would interact with players, coaches and then just again, maybe createlike a role play sort of environment so that they know that they're not going totally blind into that sort of situation.

Have you always been passionate about football?

Football was a passion of mine, even when I was younger, primary school age, we just didn't have very many female teams, so it normally meant playing with the boys and the boys teams and stuff up until I was about 14, which was the minimum age here you can join senior ladies football team, which is what I did, and played there for 14 years at a club here locally, including up until the Women's Premiership, so it was great to be involved in football, but I always loved watching football, playing football, anything to do with football, I was always there and interested.

How did you go from playing football to being a referee?

Becoming a referee for me sort of happened by chance to be honest. It was during a game, one time I got an injury, quite a bad injury to my knee and then I had seen luckily that the referee course was being advertised. So I signed up for it, but I also signed up for a coaching course pretty much at the same time, maybe about six weeks apart. I wasnât really sure which role I wanted to follow, but over that winter I had been pushed into refereeing a wee bit and said sure, why not, Iâll give it a go, it'd be a bit of extra fitness before my season restarts, and then just fell in love with it from there and never looked back.

What subjects did you study at school and university?

Coming through school I always picked PE, so I did my GCSE PE and then I also did A-level PE and then when I went onto university,I had the sport and exercise science as well within that, so I think it gives you a good understanding of obviously how your body works, and your plan and training, stuff like that as well so you know when you're working nutrition wise, things that you need to know,especially as you reach the top level, just to make sure that you're getting the most out of your body.

What are your top tips for becoming a referee?

I would say definitely give it a try for sure. You never know until you do it. I think even when I was a player, I probably never imaginedthat I would be a referee and that I would even achieve and have experienced what Iâve been able to experience. So you never knowuntil you give it a go, but it's also about probably pushing yourself out of your comfort zone, being comfortable with being uncomfortable in situations like that. It's maybe not always as bad as it probably seems it's going to be. There's probably a lot more stigma around being a referee - who wants to be a referee? - but honestly for me, it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done.

With a lifelong love of football, Louise Thompson followed her passion for the game, first as a player and now as a referee. As well as refereeing Fifa and NIFL Premiership matches, she also works for the Irish Football Association as the women's referee pathway officer, recruiting and developing up-and-coming female refs.

Louise Thompson on refereeing the Women's Irish Cup final.

If you're interested in becoming a referee, it's something you can get involved with from a young age through local referee courses. The minimum age to become a qualified referee varies depending on where in the UK you live:

In her role as a women's referee pathway officer, Louise oversees new referees right from the initial recruitment courses stage: "We then do the beginners' course with referees, giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge," she says. "We also do a hands-on part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we go through different scenariosâ¦ exactly what you do as a referee, and day-to-day practical stuff as wellâ¦ The idea is to give them all the basics and fundamentals before they go into a game so that they're prepared."

All four UK nations have established pathways for referee development and progression. Starting out at grassroots level, it's possible to progress all the way to Fifa!

Louise's first games were youth games: "I still remember my first game to this day," she says. "It was an under-13 game, and I was definitely the most nervous person on the pitch." She explains: "Over time, you'll get mentors who will come and watch you, give you advice, give you feedback" which will help you to progress to higher levels of the game.

As well as PE, Louise has found that languages are really helpful in this line of work, "especially when you're dealing with a lot of international games and people coming along," she says. "If you can learn some languages, it's very, very useful."

You could get into this role by training with a professional body.

Sources: National Careers Service, GOV.UK, FA, IFA, SFA, and FAW.

#971. Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race

Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success

Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here

In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series.

We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well).

Five years ago we had an exciting array of young players on the list, most of them 17 years old but some 16, with one youngster from Brighton being profiled like this:

double quotation markThe ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players.

It was quite an understated entry, especially compared with this one in the world section:

double quotation markThe youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17.

Borussia Dortmund’s Youssoufa Moukoko went on to play for Germany at the World Cup the following year, at the same time as Jack Hinshelwood was promoted to the Brighton Under-21s. Different trajectories, different pressures. Moukoko was already known around the world and tipped for a long career at the top. There was something completely carefree about his style, young Michael Owen-esque. Take a look at his early (and subsequent) goals in the Bundesliga here.

Then life interfered. Moukoko sustained some injuries and struggled to make the Dortmund starting XI. To be fair, he also had some decent competition up front as Erling Haaland had arrived in 2020. Moukoko had a really good spell at the start of the 2022-23 season, after Haaland had joined Manchester City, but sustained an ankle ligament tear and never quite got his starting place back.

These days Moukoko is playing in the Turkish top flight with Corum, on loan from Copenhagen, where he moved in 2025. His switch to the newly promoted Turkish top-flight side was low key with the club welcoming Moukoko to the “family” with a short statement. He is yet to start a game but his cameos off the bench have offered flashes of his quality – most notably marking his home debut with a sharp assist in a 3–0 win over Eyüpspor. His market value is €5m (£4m) reckons transfermarkt.com.

Meanwhile, Hinshelwood has made 67 Premier League appearances and was included on Thomas Tuchel’s 55-man longlist for the 2026 World Cup. A frustrating ankle injury has hampered him at the start of this campaign but his star is rising and he has a market value of €28m (£24m). Not that Brighton are about to sell him.

Neither player chose their path and whether they broke through early. They simply developed at a different pace. Hinshelwood was not ready to play top-flight football at 17; Moukoko was. Did the early exposure have a negative impact on Moukoko? It is impossible to say.

Not that it has been straightforward for Hinshelwood either. It never is. His father, Adam, told Sky this year that “it is definitely not just a straight line”, saying: “There were lots of bumps and ups and downs along the way.” There was one moment when Hinshelwood, then with the under-15s, was set a challenge to play with an older age-group, and that arguably made him as a footballer. “It was a big catalyst for Jack,” Adam said. “He rolled up his sleeves and became a proper footballer.”

Out of our 60 world talents, 24 have gone on to represent their countries. Moukoko stands on two caps, some distance behind players such as Julio Enciso and Gavi. Some have had to swap allegiances to play senior international football, such as Livano Comenencia, who started out with the Netherlands age-group teams but has more than 20 caps for Curaçao and played at this summer’s World Cup.

From our Premier League picks in 2021 astonishingly few players are with the same club. Hinshelwood is one, Liverpool’s Kaide Gordon another, but that is it. The other 18 are playing around the globe, including in the US, Qatar and Hong Kong.

The 20 players have played a total of 145 top-flight games, not a bad tally, but Hinshelwood accounts for almost half of those. Adrian Blake, who was with Watford in 2021, has carved out a very successful career in the Netherlands, having joined Utrecht in 2023. But he too, struggled in the beginning. “It hasn’t been easy and a lots of ups and downs,” he told Football-oranje.com in 2025. “But now I am getting my rewards and showing why I made the right decision by moving here.”

Blake moved to the Netherlands when he was 17. It was a huge gamble for someone so young but he says he chose the Eredivisie “because it is a great league for young players”, offering opportunities that often do not exist in England. “For me it was a no-brainer,” he said.

The 21-year-old has almost his whole career in front of him, as do Moukoko and Hinshelwood – and yet they have experienced so much already. What will the next five years bring?

#970. 'My job combines my passion for gaming and football'

Working on one of the world's biggest football video games is the perfect combination of my two biggest passions, gaming and football.

I'm CJ Ramson. I work on the creation of football video games. I work on Football Manager as an associate QA manager. QA stands for quality assurance.

We're the ones that test the game. We make sure everything works, and we work closely with the developers to try and make the most realistic simulation of football.

Growing up, I loved football, whether that was playing football or playing football video games with my friends. I'd always be doing one or the other. With the video games, the thing that really drew me to them was I've always been into the tactical side of the game, either being able to control the players or create your own tactics.

So a typical day for us, we'll get a new build in from the developers. We'll test it as a QA team, and we'll look for either bugsor ways that we can improve the game. That can be anything from the runs that players make, to decisions they make on the ball, what the team instructions and tactics do. So there's a lot of areas for us to cover. Our final goal is to make it as realistic to real football as possible.

So even though my background was in coaching, there was a lot of transferable skills that I learned and developed through my time coaching that I managed to transfer into this. So whether that's being really analytical and having a good eye for detail and knowingwhen to pick things out and what to look for, or it could be things like timekeeping and making sure things run perfectly on time, and working with other people as well. So social skills where you have to work within a team or even lead a team.

The animation he makes, and the ball physics as well, where the ball goes off after the save."

So as much as I loved playing football, I realised quite early on I probably wasn't going to be a professionalfootballer. But I wanted to work in football and find. So at college, I studied sports science, and that's where I found my love of coaching. I did my FA Level 1 and then went on to do my FA Level 2. After I left college, I got a job at Arsenal, which was unpaid, working with them, learning how to develop my coaching skills. Which then led to me having a full-time paid job at Fulham Football Club, working with the youth teams, working with the academy teams. And then that eventually led to me going to an event. I saw an opportunity where you could apply for a job in Football Manager. It was something that naturally I was interested in, had a conversation with them, and realised it was definitely something that I would love to do.

So I went to the networking event at Kick It Out, and that was an opportunity for me to network with other football coaches, other people within the gaming industries, and have a really good insight to different jobs in football gaming. Without doing that, I wouldn't have the opportunity to meet the people at Football Manager and see a new job in gaming, which I wouldn't have beenaware of.

One of the highlights of my career so far is working on the in-and-out-of-possession system on FM 26. This is something we see in real football all the time, so being part of the team that brought that to life and brought it into the game was super cool.

Working within the football industry is a dream come true. Being able to work on something that I'm passionate about, that is played and enjoyed by millions of people, is an amazing feeling for me and an amazing opportunity that I have. And yeah, I love it.

To find out what other jobs you could have in football, explore the BBC Bitesize Follow Your Passion collection.

Ever wondered who makes sure your footy video games are great? This guy!

CJ works as an associate quality assurance manager on the video game Football Manager. His team test the game to make sure everything works, and collaborate with the developers to create the most realistic simulation of football.

There are lots of different ways to progress in the gaming industry.

CJ works in the QA (Quality Assurance) team, testing games. In this team, his career progression has followed this path:

His team is just one of the options, though. "There are lots of other roles within the industry too, including production, game design, social media and development, where developers help to code the game," he explains. "Depending on your skills and interests, there are different pathways you can take that you might enjoy and be suited to."

There are different roles in video game testing. CJ notes that: "Salaries can vary depending on your role and the company you work for. They can range from around Â£20,000 to Â£50,000 and upwards." The higher salaries in this range could apply when you've gained more experienced and progressed in your career.

CJ is now a quality assurance manager, but he started out as a quality assurance tester. Find out more about the role of QA tester below. This role can have various other job titles, such as games tester, computer games tester, and video games tester.

You could get into this role via a university course, a college course (such as a Level 3 Diploma in Creative Media, an A-level in Computing, or a T-level in Digital Software Development (England only)), an apprenticeship, or applying directly if you have relevant experience.

#969. Alcaraz dominates Tiafoe in ATP Finals opener to extend winning streak

Is this the week Carlos Alcaraz gets his hands on the Nitto ATP Finals trophy? He dispatches Frances Tiafoe with Daniil Medvedev and Flavio Cobolli to come in round-robin play; You can watch the ATP Finals in Turin this week on Sky Sports Tennis

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Carlos Alcaraz powered past Frances ‌Tiafoe 6-2 6-2 in just over an hour at the ATP ‌Finals on Monday to stretch his winning run to ​10 matches.

The Spaniard is aiming for his third straight title after lifting trophies in Vienna and Paris.

He's also aiming to claim the title at the season-ending tournament for the first time after losing last year's championship match in Turin to Jannik Sinner .

Sinner, the two-time defending champion at the ATP Finals, ended his season early due to a right knee injury.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Tiafoe's baseline game was no match for Alcaraz's power and movement, with ​the world No 3 dominant from ‌the start.

Alcaraz has won three titles since returning to the tour at the US Open after a ​break of nearly five months due ⁠to a wrist injury.

The 2025 ⁠finalist quickly charged into a 4-0 lead as the American world ‌No 8 was left looking helpless against Alcaraz's versatile play.

In a near-flawless first set, ‌the Spaniard won 93 per cent of points on his first serve and a perfect 100 per cent on his second.

Before Tiafoe, making his ATP Finals debut, had time ⁠to react he was down a set ​and a break after half an ​hour.

He did earn three break points at ​3-2 but could not make them count ⁠with Alcaraz holding and breaking again after a superb rally and down-the-line winner to make it ⁠5-2. He served out the ​set in the next game.

"I would say this is the best I have felt so far in my career at this part of the season," Alcaraz said.

"I have never experienced something like this, this year. It was unusual for me, having a lot of months off the competition at home. So coming here I have a lot of energy and ambition and I am hungry for more."

"I tried to push him and let him know it is going to be a really great battle if he wants to win," Alcaraz added. "I am just really happy to start the tournament like this and hopefully I can keep it going."

Tim Henman, speaking on Sky Sports: "Alcaraz showed why he is the best and most exciting player in the world right now. Tiafoe will have to go away, lick his wounds and try to respond at this next opportunity.

"Just another incredible performance to marvel at. All aspects of Alcaraz's game firing on all cylinders."

On taking a step back in his schedule, Jamie Murray said: "Alcaraz has been quite vocal about the schedule and how he might miss more time on the tour to be fresher for the bigger tournaments.

"He is right because the calendar is so congested. The move to 12-day Masters events means players are away more, it's more mentally demanding - maybe more so than physical and he feels like he doesn't have to play every week of the year.

"He's going to decide what the biggest tournaments are for him and then he's going to try and peak for them."

#967. Ever wondered what it's like to work on Match of the Day?

With its iconic theme tune, long established time in the weekend TV schedule, and expert analysis, Match of the Day is the most famous football show in the world. Each week the team at the BBC broadcast not one, but two, episodes â bringing viewers all the latest talking points from the Premier League.

Putting on this live broadcast is no easy task, thereâs so many different jobs that get the show to air. BBC Bitesize Careers went behind the scenes on a busy Sunday afternoon to meet just a small number of people involved and to find out more about how they got their jobs on the legendary show.

Cue the music. Do, do, do, dooo, do-do-do-do doooooooâ¦.

Joe Hart on why he loves his job on Match of the Day.

From production management assistants to make up artists, assistant producers to pundits, thereâs plenty of jobs that are involved in putting Match of the Day together each week. Thatâs before mentioning the director, producer, editor, production co-ordinator, vision-mixer, sound-engineer, studio floor-manager, the list goes on. Every role requires a different set of skills and knowledge, with loving football not an essential requirement!

Isabelle Anastasiou on finding your next career step.

With a huge number of roles needed to get a live sports programme on to our screens itâs no surprise that the team at Match of the Day we spoke to all had different routes into the industry.

Some took the apprenticeship route whilst others followed their passion for a subject and went on to study it at university. Meanwhile others worked in areas away from sport, and broadcasting, getting different work experience along the way. Make sure to check out the video above to find out more

It goes to show that thereâs no one set way of doing things, and everyone has their own career path to follow. One thingâs for sure though, following your passion can be a great place to start.

Of course you might change your mind or start working in a part of the industry you didnât expect to find yourself in, maybe even change jobs along the way. Itâs all part of making your own career path, and youâll be getting skilled up and banking different experiences along the way.

#964. Why are some football shin pads so small?

Liverpool striker Lewis Koumas (second from left) sported low socks and small shinpads on his full Premier League debut at Anfield

Liverpool's Lewis Koumas made his full Premier League debut against Manchester City on Sunday.

While doing so, he sported some very low socks over what appeared to be a very small shin pad.

Last season, images of Burnley's Marcus Edwards went viral after the 27-year-old was seen wearing barely visible shin pads during a Premier League match against West Ham.

Two years ago, a picture of teenager Harry Howell celebrating with James Milner while they were Brighton team-mates also gained attention after fans noticed the visible difference in the size of their shin pads.

Howell's 'micro' pair were an obvious contrast to Milner's far more traditional-sized guards.

So what is behind the trend of extra-small shin guards, and why are they used instead of regular-sized pairs?

The simple answer is that players can choose what size shin pads they want to wear.

The International Football Association Board (Ifab), responsible for the laws of the game, say that shin pads are a mandatory piece of equipment players must wear while playing.

Be of an appropriate size to provide reasonable protection and be covered by the socks

And players are responsible for the size and suitability of their shin pads

The law does not define what an "appropriate" shin pad size is, but leave that decision to each individual player.

Shin pads provide vital protection for players to prevent serious injuries.

There has been a rising trend in younger footballers, as well as some big stars, wearing small shin pads during matches.

The reason for this could be for more comfort and to allow players to move around with greater ease.

Referees are only required to check that some form of shin guards are being worn, Ifab told BBC Sport.

Ifab said players - or the parents or guardians of youth players - must take responsibility for their own safety on the pitch.

While shin pad size is ultimately an individuals choice, any decisions around player safety would also be made in consultation with their club and medical staff.

Marcus Edwards last year was seen wearing very small shin pads for Burnley in the Premier League

Grassroots football teams have started to ban small shin pads for safety reasons.

There are concerns that small shin pads do not cover the shins properly, which can lead to an increased risk of injury - especially at non-elite level.

In August 2024, a football club banned small shin pads after a youth player suffered a double leg break.

Penistone Church player Alfie Collins broke his tibia and fibula in a tackle during a game. The teenager's shin pads, which were no bigger than a credit card, were similar to a size recently worn by some stars of the professional game.

Shin pads "play an important role in injury prevention as they are intended to protect the shin from injury", the Football Association said.

"'Micro' or 'mini' shin pads may therefore increase the risk of injury due to the smaller amount of shin covered compared to larger sized shin pads," they added.

#963. Chinese scientist sacked after child died in gene-editing trial

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Chinese authorities have sacked the researcher who led an experimental gene-editing trial that resulted in the death of a child. An investigation into the trial by the Shanghai municipal government found that the researcher and his team failed to follow regulations and overlooked warning signs in a safety report. Several others involved in the case have also been punished.

Two children died from gene therapies in China: where the field goes next

Two children died from gene therapies in China: where the field goes next

In July, the journal Science and the website Retraction Watch jointly reported that Zilong Qiu, a neuroscientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, led a team that developed an experimental gene-editing therapy for a six-year-old girl with a rare neurodevelopmental disorder called Snijders Blok–Campeau syndrome. The therapy was carried by a viral vector that was injected into the girl’s spine and then travelled to her brain. The girl died of medical complications after receiving the therapy at Xinhua Hospital, also in Shanghai, in March 2025.

The institutions involved in the trial — Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine and Xinhua Hospital — have also been reprimanded and instructed to examine their own practices. “I expect the action to send a big warning to research institutes and hospitals across the country,” says Jiayou Shi, a lawyer at the National Research Center for Civil and Commercial Law at Renmin University of China in Beijing.

The trial was conducted under China’s fast-track pathway, called investigator-initiated trials (IITs). IITs allow researchers and biotech companies to test therapies quickly in hospitals without supervision from the country’s regulators. The Chinese government increased oversight of these trials in May, which Shi says should prevent similar cases in future.

Lizzi Lee, who studies China’s economic and technological policies at the Asia Society Policy Institute, a think tank in New York City, says the trial is “a cautionary tale” for the country’s rapidly growing biotechnology industry. There is real momentum in the industry in China, but clinical oversight hasn’t always kept pace, Lee says. “The investigation is quite candid about what went wrong,” adds Lee.

According to a statement released through China’s state-run media on 13 November, the Shanghai government’s investigation found that Qiu was the main person responsible for the research. He has been sacked from his position as the deputy director of the Songjiang Research Institution, which is affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine. Another member of Qiu’s team, a deputy researcher at Xinhua Hospital, has also been dismissed. Both researchers have been barred from leading or participating in science projects for five years and have been added to a national database of people and organizations that have committed serious breaches of research integrity.

About a month before the girl received the experimental therapy, Qiu’s team received results from a preclinical toxicology study showing that monkeys sustained liver damage, according to Science and Retraction Watch. Investigators found that Qiu’s team failed to inform the researcher in charge of the clinical research at Xinhua Hospital in a timely fashion about the results of the primate experiment, which meant “the early warning signal” in the safety report was not “given high attention”, according to the statement. The clinical researcher has been removed as head of research at Xinhua Hospital. Qiu did not respond to questions about the investigation report.

Shi says the trial in the girl should not have gone ahead if the therapy showed evidence of harm in animals.

The investigators also found that Xinhua Hospital failed to conduct sufficient scientific assessment for the clinical trial. According to the statement, although the hospital’s ethics committee asked the research team to submit extra materials when safety evidence was lacking, it approved the trial without receiving those materials. In addition, the consent form given to the children’s family did not mention death as a risk of taking the therapy. Two members of the hospital’s ethics committee were given penalties.

Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine and Xinhua Hospital did not respond to questions about the investigation report.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03752-2

#962. Michael Carrick was just the latest fall guy for Manchester United’s dysfunctional hierarchy | Jamie Jackson

Disastrous decisions and confused appointments have been a constant theme at Old Trafford since Sir Alex Ferguson’s retirement in 2013

For a window into the alarming dysfunction at Manchester United that Michael Carrick failed to manage and caused his sacking, consider the case of Eddie Howe, initially a favourite to succeed the 45-year-old before Mauricio Pochettino’s emergence as the chosen one.

The former Newcastle manager had been Jason Wilcox’s choice to take over from Carrick. Howe was also the favoured candidate of Dan Ashworth, Wilcox’s predecessor as United’s director of football, to follow Erik ten Hag after the Dutchman’s sacking in October 2024. Except Wilcox disagreed and Sir Jim Ratcliffe went with Wilcox’s man, Ruben Amorim, and that December Ashworth departed only five months after joining.

At that juncture Wilcox was the technical director. Now he is United’s highest-ranking football executive, the powerbroker. He was able, apparently with a straight face, to recommend to Ratcliffe that Howe, nearly two years after he rejected him, should become United’s eighth permanent No 1 in the 13 and a half years since Sir Alex Ferguson retired.

If following this is difficult, making sense of it is near impossible. Should London’s West End need a new farce then look no further than the wacky world of Ratcliffe and the football department he leads, which is also headed up by Omar Berrada, the chief executive, and is proving a disjointed, illogical operation.

Yet if this meant Carrick was dealt a treacherous hand, it is also true that he should have played it better. This, after all, is the job of a football coach: to somehow make wine from water – even if the water is murky, and may need purifying first.

José Mourinho, one of Carrick’s predecessors, from May 2016 to December 2018, showed how – to a degree. Mourinho stated famously that leading United to second place in 2017-18 (with 81 points, 19 behind Manchester City) was one of his finest achievements. This from a serial winner who broke the United-Arsenal duopoly of the Premier League to take Chelsea to consecutive crowns (2004-05 and 2005-06), and made history in Italy by guiding Inter to the treble in 2009-10.

Mourinho’s billing of that second place was down to having to negotiate a similar shambles, overseen by Ed Woodward, the then executive vice-chair.

The Portuguese’s opening campaign ended with the Carabao Cup and Europa League collected despite, like Carrick, having to deal with a hierarchy convinced that it knew better than the man it hired as the football expert.

Here we arrive at a fundamental quality Carrick lacked: an ability to be streetwise when really required. For an example of Mourinho’s nous, rewind to a pre-season tour of America when this correspondent was offered an off-the-record sounding about a player he wanted out of the club but the executive did not.

The manager wanted his message out – that this was a player non grata. Machiavellian or pragmatic? A guess says Carrick would never dream of employing a similar tactic to achieve the best result for the team. But why not? Mourinho wanted a bad egg gone before the dressing room was stunk out and on-field prospects undermined.

Carrick, in his last month, encountered two of his own malevolents: Lisandro Martínez, a de facto captain who dared to criticise Wilcox’s recruitment after the 2-0 defeat by Atlético Madrid; and Bruno Fernandes, Carrick’s official leader, who betrayed his manager by questioning his tactics after the 4-1 humiliation at Como.

Each crossed a line and were emblematic of a chaotic changing room, a major factor in the dismal run of three wins from 15 games this season, including elimination from the Carabao Cup, and the league return of eight points from 10 matches that has United in the relegation zone.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Fernandes, Martínez and a club run like a banana republic are the next man’s problem, just as Mourinho inherited from Louis van Gaal, who was sacked the day after winning the 2016 FA Cup, the faults at boardroom level embodied by Woodward.

Here we see the recurring problem at United: a new gun is hired and is bequeathed a sorry mess that is impossible to clean up because there is no true will to eradicate it. Why? Because the only real reset of culture would be for Ratcliffe, who owns 29.4%, Wilcox, Berrada and the Glazer family, whose ownership since 2005 has left the club about £1.2bn in debt, to accept they are the problem and depart.

Carrick is a good guy whose adoration of United was returned to him by the support, underlined by the reception he got from the Stretford End after the 3-0 humbling by Bournemouth last month. Yet being a decent man and head coach was not enough.

In elite sport the fine margins are often trumpeted as the difference between triumph and failure. Last season, from mid-January, Carrick worked these his way as Manchester City, Arsenal, Liverpool and Chelsea were defeated and United lost only two of his 17 games as interim head coach.

This season, though, the fall-off was startling – and Carrick was found wanting. Who knows what might have occurred if United were the “best-in-class” organisation Ratcliffe insisted they would be under him. As with the muddled thinking regarding Howe, “worst in class” may be a more apt characterisation.

The agonising, overlong process to decide Carrick should be sacked was the latest illustration. On Monday evening the Guardian broke the news that Wilcox and Berrada would recommend to Ratcliffe that Carrick should be removed. Yet days passed during which Carrick still took training and it emerged the deal for Pochettino was being finalised. A proper functioning organisation would have acted more swiftly and with more style.

This is what the next manager has to grapple with. He may succeed. But the odds are stacked against it owing to the deep structural faults that undermine the modern Manchester United.

#961. Were any current Man City players signed during charges period?

Manchester City captain Ruben Dias has made more than 250 club appearances since his arrival in 2020

No member of Manchester City's current squad was signed during the period in which an independent commission found the club guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations.

Those offences all came between 2009 and 2018. City have denied any wrongdoing and appealed against all of the charges against them.

The club's longest-serving first-team player who was purchased from another club is Portuguese centre-back and club captain Ruben Dias, who joined from Benfica in 2020.

Norway striker Erling Haaland is the next longest-serving arrival, joining from Borussia Dortmund in the summer of 2022.

Midfielder Phil Foden is the only player to have played for the club during the period in which they breached the league's financial rules, but was not a senior signing having come through the club's youth ranks.

Foden, 26, made his first-team debut in a Champions League match against Feyenoord in November 2017.

Like Foden, versatile midfielder Rico Lewis is also a product of the club's academy but did not make his senior debut until August 2022.

All of the club's other senior players were signed between 2023 and 2026.

#959. Who is close to a yellow card suspension in Champions League?

Arsenal forward Kai Havertz is among the players to have received two yellow cards in this season's Champions League

Players will receive a one-match ban should they receive four yellow cards before the semi-finals of the Champions League.

This rule runs from the start of the league phase until the end of the quarter-finals. After then, all yellow cards are wiped out and players cannot be suspended for multiple yellow cards.

Yellow cards that result in a red card during a match do not count towards a player's tally, as a separate suspension will be served.

The same rules apply for both the Europa League and the Conference League.

During the opening three rounds of the Champions League, 16 players received two yellow cards, meaning they are now two cautions away from a one-match ban.

Shakhtar Donetsk's Marlon Gomes, Villarreal's Santiago Mourino and Inter Milan's Hakan Calhanoglu are each on three yellow cards, putting them on the brink of a ban.

Players can also be suspended if they pick up six, eight or 10 yellow cards. This would also result in a one-match suspension every time a player hits an even number of yellow cards above four.

Red cards result in a one-match suspension, with Bayern Munich's Michael Olise missing his side's earlier clash with Arsenal after being sent off against Viking in the previous round of fixtures.

Uefa may increase the length of a red card ban for serious offences such as violent conduct.

*denotes two yellows that resulted in a red card

The following players will miss the next round of league phase matches following either a yellow or red card suspension:

Matheus Cunha (Manchester United - red card suspension)

#956. Which game will Chelsea's Palmer miss after red card?

Cole Palmer was sent off in the second half of Chelsea's 2-0 loss at Stamford Bridge

Chelsea's Cole Palmer will not miss the Blues' Premier League meeting with Manchester United on Saturday, despite being sent off in his side's last Premier League match.

Palmer was shown two yellow cards in the second half of the Blues' defeat by rivals Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday. That dismissal meant that Palmer was handed a one-match ban.

The England playmaker was shown his first caution for an off-the-ball incident involving Spurs' Mateus Fernandes. He was then shown a second yellow card for a foul on Conor Gallagher.

In most cases, this would be served in that team's next Premier League match. However, Palmer will not miss Chelsea's meeting with United at Stamford Bridge.

Instead, Palmer will be banned for the Blues' EFL Cup fourth-round match away at Liverpool on Wednesday night.

This is because red card suspensions are carried out across domestic competitions rather than being specific to the competition they were received in.

Suspensions for an accumulation of yellow cards across a campaign are served in the competition in which they are received.

So while the Blues will miss Palmer for their trip to Anfield, he will be available to face United three days after the club's cup tie on Merseyside.

#955. Record-breaking Andy Robertson is Scotland’s finest captain

As he passes Kenny Dalglish’s appearance total, it is important to remember that it is the left-back’s journey that sets him apart

Andy Robertson may not be Scotland’s greatest player, but he is indisputably their finest captain. It counts as sacrilege, even to generations who have watched Kenny Dalglish only on YouTube, to reputationally place Robertson above the Liverpool hero on the basis of a cap haul that will reach 103 in St Gallen on Monday. Dalglish’s international career ended at 102 and the curious events that meant he missed the 1986 World Cup.

There is no requirement to compare a left-back in 2026 to a forward from decades earlier. Dalglish and Robertson are men in different positions in essentially a different sport. Instead, Robertson’s march to the top of the cap pile gives cause to laud his contribution.

Those within the Scotland setup regard Robertson as the glue who holds the scene together, a decorated footballer who treats everybody the same and carries out an abundance of unseen work to make this team better. Robertson has routinely paid for squad nights from his own pocket.

The 32-year-old is as dedicated to overall environment as he is to his craft. Under Robertson’s on-field guidance, Scotland have morphed from international also-rans to serial tournament participants.

Left-backs are rarely the recipients of praise. When of the status of Robertson they do, however, receive criticism when a team struggle. He has carried the heaviest load while probably unable to celebrate the highs in an appropriate manner.

Robertson’s journey sets him apart and not only from Dalglish. By March 2014, when Robertson made his debut as a 67th-minute substitute in a friendly in Warsaw, he had been rejected by Celtic’s youth system, reset his career at Queen’s Park and turned heads in Dundee United colours. Hull would come next.

“He counts as one of my best-ever signings,” says Steve Bruce, who took Robertson to Humberside. “I still remember him holding his parents’ hands when he came down.

“He could run like the wind and had such a lovely left foot. We wanted to try and sign the best young players and thought he might get a few games due to injuries but Andy went into the side and never came out, which is testament to him. I’m absolutely delighted for him.”

Robertson and Phil Bardsley replaced Alan Hutton and Barry Bannan in Poland. “He was a young boy who played with so much freedom,” Hutton says. “He had energy and aggression to go up and down the pitch all day long, he would shell crosses into the box at 100mph. For one so young, he was also amazingly good at one v one defending. I got to 50 caps. I remember thinking there would be no chance of anybody reaching 100.”

Alex McLeish, who handed Robertson the Scotland captaincy in 2018, jokes about the possible impact on Dalglish. “Kenny will want to make a comeback,” he says. “No, he will be absolutely delighted for Andy. It tells you so much about Andy’s character that someone like Kenny Dalglish is so fond of him.

“It felt to me like a new era. We were rebuilding and Andy seemed to make the most sense as being at the forefront of that. I’m pretty sure anyone else would have made the same decision. A fantastic player with a great attitude and very well liked by all his teammates. He was a natural captain. He demands high levels without being someone to blast people. He is a hard bugger; if he talks, people shut up and listen.

“When I told him [he was captain], I still remember how his eyes lit up. He loved hearing that. He gave me such a great big smile and said how honoured he would be to captain the country.”

McLeish underplays the value of his decision. Robertson has worn the armband 80 times. McLeish could easily, for example, have handed it to Kieran Tierney, Callum McGregor or John McGinn. McLeish’s faith in Robertson and convincing of Scott McTominay to commit to Scotland were huge and lasting contributions.

Robertson’s career could easily have followed an alternative path. The Scottish game is laced with players released by major clubs who spend years lurching about in its nether regions. Blair Spittal, who played with Robertson at Queen’s Park and Dundee United, believes there may be a broader lesson here. “I’m not saying every player could do the same as Andy, but within the pyramid of Scottish football there are definitely players who just need an opportunity and someone to show their belief,” he says.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“Queen’s Park at the time was a great environment for that. We were then very lucky at Dundee United to have a manager [Jackie McNamara] who believed in young players. Andy took everything in his stride. Nothing ever fazed him.”

He has made instant impressions everywhere. John Rankin was a senior player at Dundee United as Robertson elevated his reputation. He recalls a pre-season friendly at Union Berlin, when he first clapped eyes on someone who would be a Champions League winner within six years. “Who is this?” Rankin said while watching from the stand. “On his first day at the training ground, Andy bypassed the first‑team dressing room to get changed with the youth team. He was so unassuming, no entitlement about him at all.

“He knew what he wanted to do. On the pitch it was a case of: ‘Get out my road, I’m coming through.’ Off the pitch he was such a humble guy, who knew his life was built on the hard work of his parents. He had hunger to be the best player in every single session. It was never about being flash, it was about working his way to the top.”

During a game at Motherwell, with United 3-0 up, Rankin warned teammates to remain compact. Next came a marauding Robertson, who cracked home a fourth before Rankin chastised him for not following orders. “But I scored, didn’t I?” came the retort.

Jordan Henderson and James Milner have been hugely influential in shaping how Robertson deals with others. Robertson did not want Steve Clarke to call time on his Scotland managerial career in June, but during an emotional meeting in Charlotte it was clear the latter’s mind was made up. Clarke would not have returned to Hampden Park four months later but for Robertson, who was receiving recognition for 100 caps.

It is fortunate Dalglish is not protective of his record. McGinn entered this international break with 93 caps. Ryan Christie and McTominay have an outside chance of reaching 102. Billy Gilmour is 25, but hit 50 caps in October. “It’s not about now holding on to the record for ever,” Robertson says. “That’s not really me.”

Modesty. A consistent and endearing Robertson trait. Whenever this international career for the ages ends, he will be a monumental loss.

#954. Which Premier League players are set for yellow card suspensions?

Harry Maguire and Alexis Mac Allister are among 13 players on the brink of a one-match ban

The first one-match suspensions for yellow card offences in the 2026-27 Premier League season have now been served.

Hull City's Matt Crooks and Aston Villa's Matty Cash became the first players to receive a ban for accumulating five yellow cards before gameweek 19.

Players receive a one-match suspension if they pick up five or more yellow cards prior to the conclusion of their team's 19th league match of the season.

There are now 13 players sitting on four bookings after 10 rounds of matches, meaning they must avoid another yellow card prior to the halfway point of the season to avoid a ban.

Bournemouth have the most players on the brink of a ban, with three players one yellow card away from suspension.

After that date, the threshold increases to 10 yellow cards. Any player reaching that number before the end of their club's 32nd league match of the season will receive a two-match suspension.

From that point, there are further thresholds at 15 and 20 yellow cards.

For players reaching 15 cautions, they incur a three-match suspension. Punishments for players reaching 20 yellow cards are determined by a regulatory commission.

Those cut-offs do not reset until the end of the Premier League season.

In the Championship, League One and League Two, there are similar thresholds.

However, with those three divisions having 46 rounds of league matches instead of 38, players have to avoid getting 10 yellow cards before the end of the 37th league match in order to not receive a two-match suspension.

In those divisions, the yellow cards are reset at the end of the league season and do not include matches in the play-offs.

The following players have served a one-match ban and will now receive a two-match ban if they reach ten bookings before game week 32:

Matt Crooks - Hull City (five yellow cards)

If any of the following players receive another Premier League yellow card before the season's halfway point, they will be banned for one match:

Pascal Gross - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

Oliver Boscagli - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

The following players will miss their club's next set of fixtures:

Max Dowman - Arsenal (red card suspension)

Jean-Philippe Mateta - Crystal Palace (red card suspension)

Igor Thiago - Brentford (red card suspension)

The forward England star will be in attendance at the London Playing Fields Foundation’s prestigious ‘Made in London Award’ at its Gala Dinner at The Savoy on November 19

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Former England and Chelsea star Joe Cole has highlighted the vital importance of protecting grassroots pitches across the capital, warning "you can’t produce any footballers without football pitches."

The 45-year-old enjoyed an illustrious playing career, which included three Premier League titles at Stamford Bridge and 56 caps for the Three Lions, and London’s local playing fields played a pivotal role in shaping his journey to the top.

Established in 1890, the charity works to safeguard the capital’s green spaces, inspiring future generations to follow in the footsteps of sporting greats. Speaking exclusively to FourFourTwo, Cole admitted the nomination means a great deal to him.

"London and football are two of the things most dearest to my heart," Cole said. "I’m a London kid. I was born in Camden Town, and obviously football is my passion, so the two things together make perfect sense, and they do a great job there.

"We need to protect the green space, not just for football, but for every sport, for kids to play, particularly in London. We have a rich history of producing footballers. You can’t produce any footballers without football pitches – whether that be five-a-side, seven-a-side, 11-a-side, cricket pitches, anything for young people to go out and be active. It’s about keeping them off the developers and making sure there’s room for kids to play."

Renowned throughout his career for his street-footballer flair and close control, Cole honed his trademark skills growing up in north London during the 1980s, making the most of whatever space was available.

"I lived in a ground-floor flat with a tiny garden, so London was my back garden," Cole recalled. "There were no boundaries. There was a bit of grass right outside my house, a wall, and over the back end there was a little concrete seven-a-side pitch.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"You had to be imaginative. I used to walk to Market Road, which was one of the first AstroTurf pitches in the country. London is just a city riddled with little areas to play. I love London, I really do, and I can’t ever see myself living far from it."To learn more about the London Playing Fields Foundation visit lpff.org.uk

Prior to that he was the Senior Writer at BBC Match of the Day magazine. He has interviewed the likes of Harry Kane, Trent Alexander-Arnold, Gareth Southgate and attended two World Cup finals and two Champions League finals. He has been a Newcastle United season ticket holder since 2000 and has a deep knowledge on the history and culture of football shirts.
